issues.legal_issue: An Additional District Magistrate appointed with all the powers of a District Magistrate under the governing procedural law and other laws may grant permission required for a tenant-eviction suit without separate authorization from the District Magistrate.
material_facts: A landlord sought permission to bring a tenant-eviction suit that required permission from the District Magistrate.
The Provincial Government appointed an Additional District Magistrate and conferred on him all the powers of a District Magistrate under the procedural code and any other law in force.
The Additional District Magistrate granted the requested permission.
issues.conclusion: The permission was valid, and the suit was competent; the Additional District Magistrate did not need separate authorization from the District Magistrate.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(d) and 3 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, permission could be granted by the District Magistrate or an officer authorized to perform the District Magistrate’s functions. Section 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, permitted the Provincial Government to confer on an Additional District Magistrate powers under that Code or any other law. That specific power displaced the general saving language in section 1(2) of the Code. The Court held the notification conferred the relevant authority; it disapproved Kedar Nath v. Mool Chand and referred to Parthasaradhi Naidu v. Koteswara Rao on the meaning of persona designata.

issues.legal_issue: A District Magistrate identified by an eviction statute as the official responsible for granting permission is not a persona designata when the authority attaches to the office and the statutory scheme permits other officers to exercise that authority.
material_facts: The eviction statute assigned the permission function to the District Magistrate and defined that term to include an officer authorized to perform the District Magistrate’s functions.
The relevant Additional District Magistrate held a public office and had been appointed with powers under other laws, including the eviction statute.
The challenge asserted that the District Magistrate was a persona designata and that only the District Magistrate or an officer specifically authorized by that official could act.
issues.conclusion: The District Magistrate was not a persona designata; the authority was attached to the office, and the statutory scheme allowed other officers to exercise it.
issues.legal_principle: A persona designata is a person selected as an individual, rather than as the holder of an office or a member of a class. The Court applied that distinction, referring to Parthasaradhi Naidu v. Koteswara Rao, and held that an official named by virtue of office is not a persona designata where the statute permits other officers to exercise the office’s powers. Kedar Nath v. Mool Chand was disapproved.

issues.definition: In an eviction-permission proceeding, an official is not a persona designata when the authority belongs to the public office and the governing scheme allows other officers to exercise it.

issues.legal_issue: A District Magistrate’s transfer of an eviction-permission application to an Additional District Magistrate constitutes authorization for that officer to perform the permission function.
material_facts: A landlord applied to the District Magistrate for permission to bring a tenant-eviction suit.
The District Magistrate transferred the application to an Additional District Magistrate for disposal.
The Additional District Magistrate considered the application and granted permission.
issues.conclusion: The transfer could be treated as authorization for the Additional District Magistrate to exercise the District Magistrate’s permission function.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(d) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, the definition of District Magistrate included an officer authorized by the District Magistrate to perform the District Magistrate’s functions. The Court held that transferring the application to the Additional District Magistrate for disposal amounted to such authorization, while noting that it was unnecessary to rely on this ground because the government’s conferral of powers under section 10(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, was sufficient.
